api.name: reconcileConfig
api.signature: export function reconcileConfig(existing: unknown, catalog?: readonly ConfigOption[]): ConfigReconcileResult

parameters.name: existing
parameters.purpose: The whole parsed ~/.insrc/config.json document, read once by the caller. Typed `unknown` rather than a config interface because the on-disk document may predate any current shape — that is the case the Story exists to handle. Also accepts undefined/null (no file yet, i.e. the daemon first-boot path in src/daemon/index.ts).

parameters.name: catalog
parameters.purpose: Authoritative key→type→default list; defaults to CONFIG_CATALOG. Injectable so the reconciler's tests drive it from fixtures rather than the live catalog (extends the existing fixture pattern in src/config/__tests__/repo-shaper-override.test.ts:27-32).

returns.meaning: The normalized document plus the derived `changed` flag and per-key provenance lists. `changed` falls out of the same comparison that built the document — it is never recomputed by the caller, which is what makes "write back only when it changed" a property of the contract rather than of caller discipline.

errors.condition: A catalog entry declares a `type` outside the discriminant domain of ConfigOption. This is a programmer error in the catalog, not a user-config condition, and must throw rather than be silently degraded to "type mismatch → fill default", which would overwrite a legitimate user value.

preconditions: Net-new code. capability.reuse-check graded 0 of 5 candidates clear-match; no reconcile/normalize/default-fill entrypoint exists anywhere in the explored surface. src/config (partial-match, conceptScore 0.193) and src/cli/config-catalog.ts (partial-match, 0.159) are the two halves this bridges, not things it extends.
PURE: no fs, no IPC, no daemon socket, no clock. This is load-bearing — the daemon-boot call site runs before the socket exists, so the reconcile cannot be an IPC round-trip.

The caller has already read the WHOLE document. The reconciler must NOT be reached through `writeConfig(path, value)` (src/cli/services/config.ts:18-20): that seam is a per-key, single-path IPC forwarder, so N fixed keys = N round-trips and "write once only if changed" becomes unexpressible. symbol.locate found NO hit for `getByPath` / `setByPath` / `readConfig`, so the Story's premise of reusing existing dot-path get/set helpers is NOT evidenced — the dot-path get/set the catalog's `path` field implies must be located (read the config.write handler) or written inside this module.

ConfigOption's field set {path,type,default,desc} is the Story's own description, not graph-evidenced. The interface is anchored at src/cli/config-catalog.ts:23-28 (entityId 3ef0c85af2cd4247530de06874accb58) and MUST be read before the type-match predicate is written — that predicate is the whole accept-existing-vs-fill-default decision. Likewise CONFIG_CATALOG itself returned NO symbol.locate hit (coverage-gap 1): its existence, shape and entry count are unverified.
postconditions: `existing` is never mutated; `result.config` is a fresh document built by merging catalog outcomes over a deep clone of `existing`. It is a MERGE, never a rebuild from catalog entries — a catalog-driven rebuild is the single failure mode that silently drops the dynamic namespaces.

For every catalog key present in `existing` whose value satisfies the type predicate: the value is carried over unchanged (referentially preserved for objects/arrays) and its path appears in `carried`.

For every catalog key missing from `existing`: the catalog `default` is written and the path appears in `filled`. For every catalog key present but type-invalid: the catalog `default` replaces it and the path appears in `repaired`.

Every key NOT enumerable by the catalog survives verbatim, including the dynamic subtrees models.analyze.roleTiers.<roleId>, models.analyze.byRepo.<path>.*, and models.agents. This holds WITHOUT the reconciler knowing those namespaces exist, which is required: no exploration touched their on-disk shape (coverage-gap 4), so any design that must declare them would be resting on un-evidenced ground.
`changed === (filled.length + repaired.length > 0)`, and `changed === false` implies `result.config` deep-equals `existing`. Callers MUST NOT write when `changed` is false.

Non-object / unparseable `existing` (null, undefined, array, scalar) is treated as `{}` — every catalog key lands in `filled`, nothing is thrown, and the first-boot path reduces to the existing write-defaults behaviour.

parameters.name: opts

errorCases.scenario: ~/.insrc/config.json exists but cannot be read (EACCES, EISDIR, EIO — anything other than ENOENT).
errorCases.detection: The I/O side awaits `fs.readFile` inside a try/catch and branches on `err.code`: `ENOENT` is NOT an error (it is the first-boot path and degrades to `reconcileConfig(undefined)`); every other errno code falls through to the failure branch. The pure `reconcileConfig` never sees this — it has no fs.
errorCases.response: On the maintenance.update path: git-pull + build have already succeeded, so the update is NOT failed. The error is captured into `MaintenanceResult.configReconcile.error` (the `error`-present/`changed:false` shape) and one `onLog` line names the file and the errno. Nothing is written. On the daemon-boot path: log at warn, boot continues on in-memory catalog defaults, and the next boot retries.
errorCases.userImpact: The update reports success with an explicit "config not reconciled: <errno>" line rather than a silent no-op; the user's existing config is untouched. If the permission problem persists, every subsequent boot repeats the warning, so the condition is visible rather than latent.

errorCases.scenario: The config file is readable but its contents are not valid JSON (truncated by a previous crashed write, hand-edited with a trailing comma, or zero bytes).
errorCases.detection: `JSON.parse` throws `SyntaxError` inside the same try/catch that wraps the read, at the I/O boundary before `reconcileConfig` is called.
errorCases.response: Do NOT pass the raw text through and do NOT fall back to `reconcileConfig(undefined)` — that would treat a corrupt-but-recoverable document as absent and fill every catalog default over it, destroying the dynamic namespaces the Story exists to preserve. Instead: abort the reconcile, write nothing, record `configReconcile.error` with the parse message and byte offset, and emit an `onLog` line telling the user the file must be fixed or removed by hand.
errorCases.userImpact: The user is told exactly which file failed to parse and where, and that their config was left alone. The alternative (silent default-fill) would look like a successful update while having discarded models.analyze.roleTiers / byRepo / models.agents.

errorCases.scenario: A CONFIG_CATALOG entry declares a `type` value outside the ConfigOption discriminant domain (a catalog row added later with a typo'd or newly-introduced type name).
errorCases.detection: The reconciler's type-match predicate is an exhaustive `switch` over the discriminant; the unknown value reaches the `default:` arm, which is written as a throw rather than a fall-through. TypeScript makes a statically-known new discriminant a compile error at that same switch (postcondition on ConfigOption); the throw catches the case where the catalog is data the compiler cannot narrow.
errorCases.response: Throw `Error` naming the offending catalog path and the unrecognized type — this is the one error `reconcileConfig` itself raises, per the s4 contract. It must NOT degrade to "unknown type → type mismatch → fill default", which would overwrite a legitimate user value on the strength of a catalog typo.
errorCases.userImpact: A developer-facing crash during update or boot, with the bad catalog row named. This is a programmer error in our own shipped catalog, never something a user's config can trigger — no user config content can reach this branch.

errorCases.scenario: A catalog dot-path's ancestor segment collides with a non-object value in the existing document (catalog declares `models.analyze.timeout`, but the on-disk `models.analyze` is a string or a number).
errorCases.detection: The merge walk descends the dot-path segment by segment over the deep clone; before descending it checks the current node with a plain-object predicate (`typeof === 'object' && !== null && !Array.isArray`). A non-object at an intermediate segment is the collision — it is found structurally during the walk, not by pre-validating the document.
errorCases.response: Treat the whole subtree at the colliding segment as type-invalid: replace the scalar/array with an object, fill the catalog default beneath it, and record the CATALOG path in `repaired` (not the ancestor). Every sibling key that was under a *valid* ancestor is unaffected. The replaced scalar is named in the `onLog` line so the loss is stated, not hidden.
errorCases.userImpact: One malformed branch of the config is repaired and the user sees which value was discarded; the rest of the document, including the dynamic namespaces, survives untouched.

errorCases.scenario: The write-back fails after `changed === true` (disk full, EACCES, read-only home, ENOSPC mid-write).
errorCases.detection: The single `fs.writeFile` (write-temp-then-rename) rejects; the I/O wrapper awaits it inside try/catch. Because the write is the only one performed per reconcile, there is exactly one place to detect it.
errorCases.response: Capture into `MaintenanceResult.configReconcile.error` with the filled/repaired counts that were computed but not persisted, and emit the failure through `onLog`. The temp file is unlinked on failure so no partial document can be renamed into place. Do not retry in-process — daemon boot reconciles again on next start and the operation is idempotent, so a later successful run produces the identical document.
errorCases.userImpact: The update is still reported successful (git-pull + build did succeed) with an explicit line saying the config could not be written; the on-disk config remains exactly as it was — never half-written, because rename is atomic.

errorCases.scenario: The config file is modified by another process (the TUI's config.write IPC path, a second daemon, a hand edit) between this reconcile's read and its write.
errorCases.detection: `fs.stat` at read time records `mtimeMs` + `size`; the I/O wrapper re-stats immediately before the rename and compares. A difference means the snapshot `reconcileConfig` operated on is stale.
errorCases.response: Abandon the write (do not clobber the newer document), record it as a non-fatal `configReconcile.error` ("config changed during reconcile"), and log it. Because the reconcile is pure and idempotent, the correct response is to let the next trigger — daemon boot, or the next update — re-run it against the newer document rather than re-looping here.
errorCases.userImpact: A concurrent edit made from the TUI while an update is running is never silently reverted. The reconcile is deferred, not lost.

errorCases.scenario: STALE-CATALOG HAZARD (s4 precondition on `update`): the reconcile inside maintenance.update runs against the CONFIG_CATALOG the CLI process imported at startup — i.e. the PRE-update schema — making it a no-op for exactly the shape change the Story targets.
errorCases.detection: Not detectable by the reconciler itself: a reconcile against the old catalog returns a perfectly well-formed `changed: false`, which is indistinguishable from "already normalized". It is only detectable at the call site, by whether the post-build reconcile loads the catalog from the freshly built output rather than from the module graph already resident in memory. If the design resolves this via a dynamic `import()` of the newly built catalog module, THAT import rejecting (build output missing, path moved) is the detectable signal.
errorCases.response: This must be settled before implementation and is not resolvable from the s1 passes. Two acceptable resolutions: (a) `await import()` the freshly built catalog module after the build step and pass it as the `catalog` argument — the injectable second parameter exists for exactly this; on import rejection, fall back to (b). (b) Leave the authoritative reconcile to daemon boot after restart, with the update path reporting only. Either way the update path must NOT silently reconcile against the stale in-memory catalog and report a confident no-change.
errorCases.userImpact: If unresolved, the user gets an update that logs "config already up to date" while their config is missing every key the update introduced — the exact breakage the Story was written to prevent, now wearing a success message. Under resolution (b) the daemon reconciles on the next start, so the user sees a deferred, not absent, migration.

errorCases.scenario: Daemon boot's reconcile throws for any reason (catalog error, unreadable config, write failure) while the daemon is starting up.
errorCases.detection: The boot call site wraps the whole read/reconcile/write-if-changed sequence in a single try/catch. NOTE: the insertion point in src/daemon/index.ts is UNVERIFIED — no s1 exploration covered that file (coverage-gap 3) — so whether boot currently short-circuits on an existing config file must be read before this handler is placed.
errorCases.response: Never abort boot on a reconcile failure. Log at warn with the reason, continue startup with the catalog defaults applied in memory only, and leave the on-disk file untouched. The daemon owning all DB access means a daemon that refuses to start takes the CLI, MCP, and the IDE workbench down with it — a config normalization failure must not have that blast radius.
errorCases.userImpact: The daemon starts and the system stays usable; the user sees one warning line and the config is reconciled on a later boot or update once the underlying cause is fixed.

errorCases.scenario: A catalog row's own `default` value does not satisfy the row's declared `type` (a `boolean` row shipping `"false"`).
errorCases.detection: After the merge, the filled/repaired values are re-run through the SAME type-match predicate used for existing values. A default failing its own predicate is a self-inconsistent catalog row. Detected by the predicate, not by an ad-hoc second validator, so the two can never disagree.
errorCases.response: Throw with the catalog path named, in the same class as the unknown-discriminant error — a shipped catalog that cannot satisfy its own schema would otherwise make the reconcile non-idempotent (each run would see the freshly-written default as type-invalid and "repair" it again, so `changed` would be true forever and the file would be rewritten on every boot).
errorCases.userImpact: Caught in our own test suite, not by users — the reconciler's tests drive the catalog from fixtures via the injectable `catalog` parameter and can assert this holds for the real CONFIG_CATALOG.

edgeCases.input: `existing` is `undefined` or `null` — no ~/.insrc/config.json on disk (daemon first boot).
edgeCases.expected: Treated as `{}`. Every catalog key lands in `filled`, `carried` and `repaired` are empty, `changed === true`, and exactly one write occurs. Reduces exactly to the existing first-boot default-writer behaviour in src/daemon/index.ts — the boot path gets no new semantics, only a wider one.

edgeCases.input: `existing` parses to a non-object: an array, a string, a number, or `true`.
edgeCases.expected: Treated as `{}` per the s4 postcondition — nothing thrown, all catalog keys filled, `changed === true`. Note the deliberate asymmetry with the corrupt-JSON error case: a document that parses to the wrong JSON *type* carries no recoverable user data, whereas one that fails to parse may.

edgeCases.input: A config already fully normalized — every catalog key present and type-valid, nothing extra.
edgeCases.expected: `carried` holds every catalog path, `filled` and `repaired` are empty, `changed === false`, `result.config` deep-equals `existing`, and NO write is performed. This is the steady-state case: every boot after the first hits it.

edgeCases.input: The same reconcile run twice back to back: `reconcileConfig(reconcileConfig(x).config)`.
edgeCases.expected: Second call returns `changed === false` for all x — the idempotence postcondition. This is what makes the daemon-boot reconcile safe to run unconditionally on every start, and what makes a deferred reconcile (stale-catalog resolution (b)) converge to the same document.

edgeCases.input: A config carrying values in all three dynamic namespaces the catalog cannot enumerate: `models.analyze.roleTiers.<roleId>`, `models.analyze.byRepo.<absolute path>.*`, and `models.agents` — alongside a catalog that has since gained and lost keys.
edgeCases.expected: All three subtrees are byte-identical after reconcile; only catalog-enumerable keys change. The reconciler achieves this WITHOUT knowing those namespaces exist, because it merges over a deep clone rather than rebuilding from catalog rows. No s1 exploration touched their on-disk shape (coverage-gap 4), so any design that had to name them would rest on un-evidenced ground. This is the single case most worth an explicit acceptance criterion (the Story ships with `acceptanceCriteria: []`).

edgeCases.input: A catalog-enumerated key whose existing value is falsy-but-valid: `false`, `0`, `""`, `[]`, or `{}`.
edgeCases.expected: Carried, never filled. The missing/present test must be key existence (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty` on the resolved parent), NOT truthiness — a truthiness check would silently reset every user who deliberately disabled a boolean flag or cleared a list.

edgeCases.input: A catalog key whose existing value is `null` for a non-nullable declared type (e.g. an `object`- or `string`-typed row).
edgeCases.expected: Type-invalid → `repaired` with the catalog default, since `typeof null === 'object'` would otherwise let a null slip through an object-type predicate and be carried as a valid value. The predicate must reject `null` explicitly. If the discriminant domain (read from src/cli/config-catalog.ts:23-28) turns out to include a nullable type, that row's predicate accepts it and it is carried instead.

edgeCases.input: A catalog key whose existing value is an object matching the declared type but carrying extra sub-keys the catalog does not enumerate.
edgeCases.expected: Carried unchanged and referentially preserved — the extra sub-keys survive. The reconciler does not recurse INTO a type-matching object to prune it; the catalog enumerates dot-paths, and a path that matches at its own level is terminal for this decision.

edgeCases.input: A catalog dot-path whose ancestor chain is only partially present (catalog has `models.analyze.timeout`; existing has `models` but no `models.analyze`).
edgeCases.expected: The missing intermediate objects are created during the walk and the default is written at the leaf; only the leaf catalog path appears in `filled`, never the synthesized ancestors. Sibling keys under `models` are untouched.

edgeCases.input: An empty catalog, or a catalog with zero entries matching anything in the document (also the reconciler's tests driving `catalog` from a minimal fixture).
edgeCases.expected: `changed === false`, `result.config` deep-equals `existing`, no write. The `catalog` parameter being injectable is what lets the tests exercise this without touching the live CONFIG_CATALOG — extending the fixture pattern at src/config/__tests__/repo-shaper-override.test.ts:27-32.

edgeCases.input: A key that exists in the document at a catalog path but where the document ALSO has a sibling dynamic key at the same level (e.g. catalog owns `models.analyze.roleTiers` defaults while `models.analyze.byRepo.<path>` sits beside it).
edgeCases.expected: The catalog key is reconciled and the dynamic sibling is preserved — the two decisions are independent because the merge writes only at resolved catalog paths and copies everything else. This is the case a naive "reconcile the `models` subtree" implementation gets wrong.

edgeCases.input: A catalog key present, type-valid, and already exactly equal to the catalog default.
edgeCases.expected: `carried`, not `filled` — and `changed` stays false on its account. The distinction matters for the log line: reporting it as "filled" would make every steady-state boot claim it migrated something.

Keep the module free of fs, IPC, socket and clock access — the daemon-boot caller runs before the socket exists. Land it unwired: at this point it is inert and no runtime behaviour has changed.

Add tests as siblings in src/config/__tests__/, extending the existing on-disk-fixture pattern at src/config/__tests__/repo-shaper-override.test.ts:27-32 rather than inventing a harness, and driving the catalog through the injectable parameter instead of the live one. Cover: carried/filled/repaired classification; the captured real-world fixture from step 2 emerging with all three dynamic namespaces byte-identical; idempotency (a second reconcile reports changed === false); changed === false implying deep-equality with the input; and the non-object/absent input degenerating to a full fill with nothing thrown. Treat the dynamic-namespace-preservation case as the acceptance criterion the Story currently lacks (acceptanceCriteria: []).

Decide the ConfigStore wrapper on the evidence gathered in step 1. If ConfigStore already owns both a whole-document read and a whole-document write, add a thin reconcile method there so the read-whole / reconcile / write-once-if-changed sequence lives in one place and cannot drift between the two call sites; otherwise skip it and let each call site perform its own read/reconcile/write-if-changed, accepting the duplication as a documented maintainability cost (not a correctness gap — `changed` guards the write on both paths). Either way reconcileConfig's signature and semantics are unchanged, so this decision does not gate the steps that follow.

Wire daemon boot first, as the authoritative reconcile point: change the first-boot default writer in src/daemon/index.ts from write-defaults-if-absent to read-whole → reconcile → write-once-if-changed, resolving the file location through globalConfigDirs. The absent-file case must reduce exactly to today's write-defaults behaviour so first boot is unchanged. This is the first step that alters an existing installation's on-disk document; land it before the update-path wiring so that even if the CLI side is deferred, every installation still normalizes on its next daemon start.

Settle the stale-catalog hazard on the update path before wiring it, since it is not resolvable from the s1 passes: maintenance.update runs inside a CLI process that loaded the PRE-update CONFIG_CATALOG at import time, so reconciling in-process against that module reconciles against the old schema and is a no-op for precisely the shape change this Story targets. Choose one — import the freshly built catalog module after the build step so the reconcile sees the new schema, or leave the authoritative reconcile to daemon boot after restart and have the update path only report. Record the choice and its rationale with the code.

Add the optional `configReconcile` summary field to MaintenanceResult — additive only, changing no existing field's meaning — carrying changed plus filled/repaired counts and an optional error string, with the optionality written explicitly per exactOptionalPropertyTypes. Counts only; the per-key dot-path detail goes to onLog.

Wire the reconcile into maintenance.update, sequenced strictly after git-pull and build and never before, per the resolution from step 9. Add no new option — reconciliation is unconditional, not opt-in, since a config left un-reconciled after an update is the exact breakage this Story prevents. Reuse the existing onLog channel for exactly one reconcile line (filled/repaired counts, or an explicit no-change line — a silent no-op is not acceptable output). Treat a reconcile failure as non-fatal: git-pull and build already succeeded, so capture the error in configReconcile.error, surface it through onLog, and rely on daemon boot to reconcile on next start. Write the file at most once per update and only when changed.

Validate end-to-end on a scratch copy of the captured step-2 fixture: run an update against it, diff the resulting file against the pre-change capture, and confirm the newly-catalogued key was added, the type-invalid key was repaired, every dynamic namespace is byte-identical, and a second run performs no write at all. Then confirm the same on the daemon-boot path. No further backfill exists to run — normalization is lazy and per-installation, occurring on each machine's next boot or update.

migration.backwardCompat: Four existing surfaces are touched, each kept compatible by construction. (1) CONFIG_CATALOG / ConfigOption relocation: the old module path src/cli/config-catalog.ts survives as a re-export of both symbols, so every existing importer compiles unchanged and zero call sites churn. This matters more than usual here — import.graph returned totalInDegree 0 with empty importer lists, so the real importer set is unknown, and the shim is what makes it safe not to know. Neither symbol changes shape: no ConfigOption field is added, removed or retyped, and no catalog entry value changes. (2) MaintenanceResult: the configReconcile field is additive and optional, so existing readers of the result — including any IDE-side consumer — are untouched and no current field changes meaning. The git-pull + build behaviour of maintenance.update is otherwise unchanged, and a reconcile failure does not turn a successful update into a failed one. (3) The daemon boot contract: an absent config file still produces exactly today's written defaults; only the previously-unhandled existing-file case gains behaviour. (4) The on-disk ~/.insrc/config.json is forward- and backward-tolerable across the change. A normalized document differs from its predecessor only by keys the new catalog declares, carrying values an older build would have resolved to its own defaults anyway, and every key an older build wrote — catalog-known or dynamic — survives verbatim. A user who reverts to a pre-change build after normalization therefore reads a config it understands; no data rollback accompanies a code rollback. The reconcile is deliberately NOT routed through writeConfig(path, value) at src/cli/services/config.ts:18-20: that per-key IPC forwarder would make N fixed keys N round-trips and would make "write once only if changed" unexpressible, and it is unusable from daemon boot, which runs before the socket exists. That seam's own contract is left untouched for its existing callers.

alternativesConsidered.name: Pure reconcile function over the whole document (catalog relocated to src/config)
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: CONFIG_CATALOG moves to src/config; a pure `reconcileConfig(doc, catalog) -> { config, report }` does all schema work in memory, and each caller owns its own read/write-if-changed.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Relocate the key→type→default catalog from src/cli/config-catalog.ts to a daemon-safe shared module under src/config (src/cli re-exports it so existing CLI imports keep compiling), and add a sibling pure module exposing one function: `reconcileConfig(current: unknown, catalog: readonly ConfigOption[]): ReconcileResult`. `ReconcileResult` is `{ config: ConfigDocument; changed: boolean; report: { filled: string[]; retyped: string[]; carriedOver: number; preservedUnknown: string[] } }`. The function is a MERGE over a structural clone of the existing document — never a rebuild from catalog entries — so any key the catalog cannot enumerate (models.analyze.roleTiers.<roleId>, models.analyze.byRepo.<path>.*, models.agents) survives untouched by construction rather than by an explicit allow-list. It performs no I/O and touches no IPC: dot-path get/set are internal helpers, `changed` is computed inside, and the two wiring targets (maintenance.update, daemon boot) each do read-whole → reconcile → write-once-only-if `changed`. maintenance.update reports through its existing `onLog: LogFn` channel and folds the report into `MaintenanceResult`; boot reuses the same call in place of its current write-if-absent.
pros: Idempotence is a property of the contract, not of the caller: `changed` is derived from the same comparison that produced the document, so a no-op update cannot write.

Preserve-unknown-keys — the acceptance requirement with the least evidence behind it — is guaranteed structurally by merging over the existing document, with no dependence on knowing the dynamic namespaces in advance.
Avoids the weak seam the Story assumed: no N-round-trip `writeConfig(path, value)` per fixed key, so the whole reconcile is one atomic file write.
Pure and I/O-free, so the reconciler is testable with plain in/out fixtures in the existing src/config/__tests__ sibling directory, with no daemon, socket, or on-disk harness.
Generic by shape — a future catalog entry needs no migration code, only a new ConfigOption row.
cons: Requires the relocation the Story only asks us to "consider", and the import.graph evidence for that move is unresolved (in-degree 0 is absent evidence, not a clear field), so the move must be justified by src/config's independence and verified by direct reading of src/daemon imports.
Two callers each re-implement read-whole and write-once, so the atomic-write discipline is duplicated and can drift between the CLI update path and daemon boot.
The reconciler does not own the file, so nothing prevents a third future caller from doing a partial write that bypasses reconciliation.
Structural clone + full-document diff is more work per boot than a targeted key check, though at config-file scale this is negligible.
alternativesConsidered.rationale: No Story acceptance criteria, HLD shared contracts, or Epic constraints were supplied to this step, so constraintScore is empty rather than populated with invented IDs; scoring falls back to the acceptance bar the alternatives themselves state — idempotence (no write on a no-op), preservation of unenumerable keys across a shape change, and a single atomic write. a1 is the only option that satisfies all three structurally rather than by discipline: `changed` is derived from the same comparison that produced the document, so a no-op cannot write; preservation of models.analyze.roleTiers.*, models.analyze.byRepo.*, and models.agents holds by merging over a clone of the existing document, which requires no advance knowledge of those namespaces — the exact surface s1's coverage-gap bundle flags as un-evidenced; and the reconcile is one file write rather than N writeConfig round-trips. Its real cost is that read-whole/write-once is duplicated across maintenance.update and daemon boot, so the atomic-write discipline can drift, and nothing structurally prevents a third caller from bypassing reconciliation. That is a maintainability risk, not a correctness gap against the stated bar, and it is the cheapest risk to retire later (a3's method can wrap this function without changing it). The relocation to src/config is required, and its evidence is weak (in-degree 0 is absent evidence, not a clear field) — implementation must verify by reading src/daemon imports directly before committing the move.

alternativesConsidered.name: Reconcile as a method on the existing ConfigStore (file owner keeps the read-modify-write)
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Add `reconcile(catalog): Promise<ReconcileReport>` to the existing ConfigStore in src/config/store.ts, so the component that already owns the config file also owns the atomic read → normalize → conditional write.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Rather than exposing a free function and leaving I/O to callers, extend the existing on-disk owner. ConfigStore (src/config/store.ts, the highest-ranked near-miss in s1's concept.resolve) gains one method: `reconcile(catalog: readonly ConfigOption[]): Promise<ReconcileReport>`, where `ReconcileReport = { changed: boolean; filled: string[]; retyped: string[]; preservedUnknown: string[] }`. The pure merge logic still lives in its own module so it stays unit-testable, but the public contract callers see is the store method — one call, one atomic read-modify-write, no way to reconcile without going through the file's owner. The catalog still relocates to src/config (the store must import it without reaching into src/cli). maintenance.update and daemon boot both become a single `await store.reconcile(CONFIG_CATALOG)` plus report rendering.
pros: Single owner of the config file performs the read-modify-write, so the atomic/idempotent guarantee lives in one place and cannot drift between the two call sites.
Smallest public surface of any option: one method plus one report type; callers need no knowledge of dot-paths, merge rules, or change detection.
Sits naturally beside the existing store primitives rather than introducing a parallel path to the same file, avoiding two components that both know how to write config.json.
Trivially extends to a third caller later — anyone holding a store can reconcile correctly by construction.
cons: Couples the storage component to the schema catalog, giving the store a dependency it does not have today and mixing 'how the file is persisted' with 'what the file should contain'.
ConfigStore's actual read/write primitives are a near-miss inference from s1, not confirmed; the method may not fit its current shape and the file must be read before committing.
Tests must exercise the method through the store's I/O, so the fast pure-fixture path exists only for the inner merge module, not the shipped contract.
Slightly harder to reuse the normalization in a non-store context (e.g. validating a config before it is written).
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Meets the same three properties as a1 and is strictly better on the one axis a1 loses: the file's owner performs the read-modify-write, so idempotence and atomicity live in one place and cannot drift between the CLI update path and daemon boot, and a future third caller is correct by construction. It also has the smallest public surface — one method plus one report type. It ranks second only because it rests on an unconfirmed premise: ConfigStore's read/write primitives are a near-miss inference from s1's concept.resolve, not verified, so the method may not fit the store's current shape. It also couples the persistence component to the schema catalog, mixing 'how the file is persisted' with 'what it should contain', and pushes the shipped contract behind I/O so only the inner merge module keeps the fast pure-fixture test path. If reading src/config/store.ts confirms the store already owns a whole-document read and write, this becomes the better choice and the delta from a1 is small — a1's pure function moves inside the method unchanged.

alternativesConsidered.name: Daemon-owned `config.reconcile` IPC operation
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Expose reconciliation as a new daemon IPC method returning a report, keeping every config write inside the daemon and making the CLI update path a thin caller.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Treat reconciliation as a daemon capability rather than a shared library. Add a `config.reconcile` JSON-RPC method whose result is `{ changed: boolean; filled: string[]; retyped: string[]; preservedUnknown: string[] }`. The handler does the read-whole / merge / write-once-if-changed in-process; the catalog relocates to src/config so the daemon can import it without depending on src/cli. Daemon boot invokes the handler function directly (no socket hop); maintenance.update calls the IPC and renders the returned report through its existing `onLog` channel into `MaintenanceResult`. This keeps the repo's stated rule that the daemon owns persistent state and that CLI/MCP reach it only over IPC, and gives the reconcile outcome a stable wire shape any client (CLI, MCP, IDE) can consume.
pros: Consistent with the architectural rule that the daemon owns on-disk state and clients go through IPC — the CLI never writes config.json itself.
The report becomes a versioned wire contract available to every client, including the IDE, not just the two call sites this Story wires.
One implementation, one owner, one atomic write; boot and update share the exact same handler code path.
Replaces the per-key `writeConfig` round-trip pattern with a single call, directly resolving the seam problem s1 flagged.
cons: Ordering hazard on the update path: maintenance.update git-pulls and rebuilds, so the daemon may be stopped, mid-restart, or running pre-update code exactly when the CLI wants to reconcile — the one moment the IPC is least reliable.

A reconcile that must run at boot cannot depend on the socket being up, so the handler must be callable in-process anyway, meaning the IPC layer is additive surface over a function that has to exist regardless.
Adds a wire contract (and its mirrored types) for what the Story scopes as internal behaviour, raising the cost of later changes to the report shape.
Testing requires an IPC harness for the shipped contract rather than plain fixtures.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Correct on ownership philosophy — the daemon owning on-disk state and clients reaching it over IPC matches the repo's architectural rule, and a versioned wire report would serve the IDE as well as the CLI. It fails on sequencing, which is decisive here. maintenance.update git-pulls and rebuilds, so the daemon is plausibly stopped, mid-restart, or running pre-update code at precisely the moment the CLI needs to reconcile — the least reliable moment for the socket. Worse, boot reconciliation cannot wait on the socket at all, so the handler must be directly callable in-process regardless; the IPC layer is therefore additive surface over a function that has to exist either way, and a1/a3 ship that function without the extra contract. It also converts internal behaviour into a wire shape with mirrored types, raising the cost of later report-shape changes, and forces an IPC harness to test the shipped contract instead of plain fixtures. Ranked above a2 because its risks are cost and operational ordering, not the possibility of corrupting user config.

alternativesConsidered.name: Catalog extended to declare dynamic namespaces (schema covers both enumerable and open-ended keys)
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Widen the catalog data model with a `ConfigNamespace { prefix, valueType }` declaration alongside `ConfigOption`, so dynamic subtrees are schema-described and validated rather than merely preserved.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Keep a1's pure-function seam but change the authoritative data model. The schema becomes a pair: `ConfigOption { path, type, default, desc }` for enumerable keys plus `ConfigNamespace { prefix, keyKind, valueType, desc }` for open-ended ones — `models.analyze.roleTiers.*`, `models.analyze.byRepo.*`, `models.agents.*` become declared entries rather than an unenumerable residue. `reconcileConfig` then classifies every leaf into exactly three buckets: catalog-known (carry over if type-matches, else fill default), namespace-known (carry over if the value matches the namespace's declared valueType, else record as invalid), and genuinely-unrecognized (preserve verbatim, report). The report gains a `namespaceEntries` count and an `invalidNamespaceValues` list. The schema thereby describes the entire config surface, and "unknown" narrows to only truly foreign keys.
pros: The config schema becomes complete and self-describing — the dynamic namespaces stop being a special case the reconciler must not break and become a first-class part of the data model.
Catches corruption inside dynamic subtrees (e.g. a roleTier holding a non-tier value) that a1 would carry over unexamined.
The same namespace declarations are reusable by other config consumers — validation, the CLI config surface, and docs — not just this reconciler.
Still merge-based, so foreign keys outside every declared namespace are preserved.
cons: Changes a shared catalog type that other config surfaces read, widening the blast radius well beyond this Story's stated internal scope.

Requires knowing the on-disk shape of the three dynamic namespaces — precisely the surface s1's coverage-gap bundle flags as entirely un-evidenced — so the design cannot be finalized without a verification pass first.
A wrong or incomplete namespace declaration is actively worse than no declaration: it can reject a legitimate value that a1's blind preservation would have kept.
Highest-cost option for a Story whose acceptance bar is "a shape change never breaks an existing installation", which a1 already meets.
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: The most ambitious and the worst fit for this Story's bar. It depends on knowing the on-disk shape of models.analyze.roleTiers.*, models.analyze.byRepo.*, and models.agents — the one surface s1 identifies as entirely un-evidenced — so the design cannot be finalized without a verification pass that none of the other options require. That dependency inverts the acceptance property: a wrong or incomplete ConfigNamespace declaration can reject a legitimate existing value that a1's blind merge would have preserved, so the mechanism intended to strengthen the schema is the one mechanism that can actively break an existing installation on a shape change. It also widens the blast radius by changing a shared catalog type other config surfaces read, well beyond the Story's stated internal scope, at the highest cost estimate (L) for a bar a1 already clears at M. The idea has genuine long-term value — validating inside dynamic subtrees, and reusable namespace declarations for the CLI config surface and docs — but it belongs in a follow-up once those namespaces are actually characterized, layered on top of a1's or a3's merge, not as this Story's first move.
